United States District Court, [Sample Jurisdiction]

MEMORANDUM IN SUPPORT OF MOTION TO SUPPRESS STATEMENTS
(SAMPLE excerpt for citation verification only. Not legal advice. Not a court filing.)

I. Custodial interrogation requires the Miranda warnings.

The privilege against compelled self-incrimination applies in the stationhouse, not only at trial. A person taken into custody and interrogated must be warned of the right to remain silent and the right to counsel. Miranda v. Arizona, 384 U.S. 436 (1966). The Court had already begun to police interrogation without counsel in Escobedo v. Illinois, 378 U.S. 478 (1964). The right to appointed counsel in serious prosecutions is separately secured. Gideon v. Wainwright, 372 U.S. 335 (1963).

Congress later attempted a totality-of-the-circumstances substitute for the warnings. 18 U.S.C. § 3501. The Court held that Miranda announced a constitutional rule that Congress may not overrule legislatively. Dickerson v. United States, 530 U.S. 428 (2000). Later cases address subsequent statements after an unwarned admission. Oregon v. Elstad, 470 U.S. 298 (1985). Invocation of counsel during interrogation also has a specific follow-up rule. Edwards v. Arizona, 451 U.S. 477 (1981).

Initial appearance procedure is addressed in Fed. R. Crim. P. 5. The privilege itself is U.S. Const. amend. V.
